--- pagetitle: "From Data to Plot" # Experimental animated explainer: read, clean, model, plot. The plot slide is animated in # the style of Emil Hvitfeldt's ggplot2-deconstructed (tidy-animations). # One deck per animation: the animation code is in ggplot2-ols-anim.html. format: revealjs: theme: [default, ../slides.scss] width: 1280 height: 720 slide-number: false hash-type: number code-overflow: wrap code-line-numbers: false footer: "Quantitative Methods I · From data to plot · experimental" include-after-body: - ggplot2-ols-anim.html # not ggplot2-ols.html: that name is the render output execute: echo: false knitr: opts_chunk: comment: "" # results print plainly, as in the Console (like the recap slides) collapse: false # each result appears below the code that produced it --- ## 1. Read the data :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(dplyr) dataset <- read.csv("data/ess_lab.csv") # the two variables we need dataset |> select(eduyrs, lrscale) |> head() ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` eduyrs lrscale 1 12 5 2 14 0 3 16 3 4 14 5 5 12 2 6 16 4 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%" .fe-note} - European Social Survey, round 11: one row per respondent, 39,514 rows - `eduyrs`: years of education - `lrscale`: left-right self-placement, 0 = left, 10 = right - Both use 77, 88, 99 for missing answers ::: :::: ## 2. Clean :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="58%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # missing codes become NA dataset$lrscale_clean <- ifelse( dataset$lrscale %in% c(77, 88, 99), NA, dataset$lrscale ) # keep 4 to 24 years (the rest becomes NA) dataset$edu <- ifelse( dataset$eduyrs >= 4 & dataset$eduyrs <= 24, dataset$eduyrs, NA ) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="42%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # check range(dataset$lrscale_clean, na.rm = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0 10 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} range(dataset$edu, na.rm = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4 24 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fe-note} - Always check after cleaning: 0 to 10, and 4 to 24 - Outside 4 to 24 years: 1.5% of respondents. Dropping them keeps the plot readable ::: ::: :::: ## 3. Model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} model <- lm(lrscale_clean ~ edu, data = dataset) summary(model) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 5.59064 0.04622 121.0 <2e-16 *** edu -0.03562 0.00334 -10.7 <2e-16 *** ``` ::: ::: ## 4. Plot: how a ggplot is built {.ol-slide} :::::: {.columns} ::::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ggplot2) dataset |> ggplot(aes(x = edu, y = lrscale_clean)) + stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point") + geom_smooth(method = "lm") + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(4, 24, 4)) + labs( x = "Years of education", y = "Left-right (0 = left, 10 = right)" ) + theme_minimal(base_size = 21) ``` ::: :::: {.ol-captions} ::: {.ol-cap data-stage="0"} Each `+` adds one piece. ::: ::: {.ol-cap data-stage="1"} Lay the plot down… ::: ::: {.ol-cap data-stage="2"} …and pull it apart: one card per block of code. ::: ::: {.ol-cap data-stage="3"} `dataset |> ggplot(aes(...))`: the data and the mapping, `edu` on x and `lrscale_clean` on y. This sets up the axes. ::: ::: {.ol-cap data-stage="4"} `stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point")`: one dot per year of education, the mean left-right position of everyone with that many years. ::: ::: {.ol-cap data-stage="5"} `geom_smooth(method = "lm")`: the regression line from step 3 (slope -0.036), fitted on all respondents, not on the dots. Grey band: its 95% confidence interval. ::: ::: {.ol-cap data-stage="6"} `scale_x_continuous()`: puts the x axis numbers at 4, 8, …, 24. ::: ::: {.ol-cap data-stage="7"} `labs()`: the axis titles. ::: ::: {.ol-cap data-stage="8"} `theme_minimal()`: the look. Here: no grey background, light grid lines, and text size 21. ::: ::: {.ol-cap data-stage="9"} Stack the cards again… ::: ::: {.ol-cap data-stage="10"} …and it is one plot. ::: :::: ::::: ::::: {.column width="50%"} ```{=html}
``` ::::: :::::: []{.fragment .ol-frag}[]{.fragment .ol-frag}[]{.fragment .ol-frag}[]{.fragment .ol-frag}[]{.fragment .ol-frag}[]{.fragment .ol-frag}[]{.fragment .ol-frag}[]{.fragment .ol-frag}[]{.fragment .ol-frag}[]{.fragment .ol-frag} ## 5. Make it publication ready {.pub-slide} :::::: {.columns} ::::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dataset |> ggplot(aes(x = edu, y = lrscale_clean)) + stat_summary( fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 3, colour = "grey55" ) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "black") + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(4, 24, 4)) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 10)) + labs( x = "Years of education", y = "Left-right (0 = left, 10 = right)" ) + theme_minimal( base_size = 21, base_family = "serif" # optional: a Times-like font ) + theme( panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), axis.line.x = element_line(colour = "black") ) ``` ::: ::::: ::::: {.column width="50%"} :::: {.pub-captions} ::: {.pub-cap data-stage="0"} We can make a couple of small fixes: ::: ::: {.pub-cap data-stage="1"} **1\.** Data in the background: bigger grey dots ::: ::: {.pub-cap data-stage="2"} **2\.** The result in front: a black line (prints in greyscale too) ::: ::: {.pub-cap data-stage="3"} **3\.** Less ink: only horizontal grid lines, and a baseline ::: ::: {.pub-cap data-stage="4"} **4\.** The whole 0 to 10 scale: from 4 to 24 years, the line drops only 0.7 points. Significant, but small. `coord_cartesian()` zooms without dropping data. ::: ::: {.pub-cap data-stage="5"} No title inside the figure: in a journal, it goes in the caption. ::: ::: {.pub-cap data-stage="6"} **5\.** Optional: `base_family = "serif"` for a Times-like font, to match a paper in Times New Roman. Many journals want sans serif in figures: check their guidelines. ::: :::: ```{=html}
``` ::: {.pub-figcap} **Figure 1.** Left-right self-placement by years of education. Dots: mean per year. Line: OLS fit with 95% confidence interval (N = 33,589). Data: European Social Survey, round 11. ::: ::::: :::::: []{.fragment .pub-frag}[]{.fragment .pub-frag}[]{.fragment .pub-frag}[]{.fragment .pub-frag}[]{.fragment .pub-frag}[]{.fragment .pub-frag} ## 6. Export {.export-slide} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the plot from step 5 in an object, # with print-size text (11 pt) p <- dataset |> ggplot(aes(x = edu, y = lrscale_clean)) + # ... the other layers from step 5 ... theme_minimal(base_size = 11) # for the paper: PDF (vector, sharp at any zoom), # with the fonts embedded ggsave( "figure1.pdf", p, width = 16, height = 11, units = "cm", device = cairo_pdf ) # for Word or slides: PNG ggsave("figure1.png", p, width = 16, height = 11, units = "cm") ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%" .fe-note} - Save at the size it will be printed: one column is about 8 cm, a full page about 16 cm. Then 11 pt in R is 11 pt in the paper - PDF for the paper: lines and text stay sharp. `cairo_pdf` embeds the fonts, so it looks the same on every machine and printer - PNG (300 dpi by default) for Word and slides - Not the Export button of the Plots pane: the size depends on your window - Check the journal's guidelines: some ask for TIFF or EPS ::: :::: ## Getting started :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="40%"} **Install** (once per computer) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} install.packages("ggplot2") ``` ::: **Load** (every session) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ggplot2) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="60%" .ol-links} **Learn more** - [ggplot2 website](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/): reference for every function, and [where to start learning](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/#learning-ggplot2) - [Cheat sheet: Data visualization with ggplot2](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/html/data-visualization.html) - *R for Data Science* (2e): [Data visualization](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-visualize) and [Communication](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/communication) (titles, labels, themes) - [*R Graphics Cookbook*, 2nd edition](https://r-graphics.org/) (Winston Chang): one recipe per plot problem - [*ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis*](https://ggplot2-book.org/) (3e): how ggplot2 works inside **The theory** - [*The Grammar of Graphics*](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/0-387-28695-0) (Leland Wilkinson, 2005): the idea behind ggplot2's layers ::: ::::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
